title: Retention fade-case probe: long-context retrieval stress (8k / 32k / 128k)
content:
Purpose: quick notes + running log for a focused probe we called the 'retention fade-case'. Goal is to exercise retrieval + KV cache + attention sink failure modes across 8k / 32k / 128k contexts and produce a compact set of prompt cases that reliably expose recall erosion, truncation artifacts, and attention reallocation when the model is forced to attend over many retrieved chunks.

High-level hypothesis:
- When retrieval chains include many long, overlapping passages, the effective useful prefix retained in KV cache degrades non-linearly as context grows (not just linear truncation).
- This manifests as: hallucinated citations, loss of entity coreference after deterministic anchor passes, and sudden token-level perplexity jumps at boundary regions (prefix boundaries + retrieval insertion points).
- Attention sink tests (dense repeated tokens / high-entropy markers) will cause disproportionate KV eviction behavior leading to downstream recall loss.

Experiment design (RF-001):
- Model candidates: open-model-v2-16k, open-model-v2-64k, experimental-quant-128k (quant shim) — run all at same temperature/top-p settings.
- Context sizes: target windows of ~8k, ~32k, ~128k tokens. For 128k runs use chunked retrieval + streaming injection to simulate real retrieval load.
- Retrieval patterns: 1) Sparse: 10 non-overlapping docs (long each); 2) Dense-chained: 40 overlapping 2–3 paragraph snippets with 30–60% overlap; 3) Adversarial-sink: embed repeated high-entropy noise paragraphs every Nth retrieved doc (N = 5, 10) to exercise attention saturation.
- Prompts: anchor paragraph (ground-truth facts), follow-up Qs that require citing a single specific paragraph index (e.g., "Which paragraph defines the term X? cite paragraph id"). We measure exact-match of citation ID and answer correctness.

Metrics (observed and targets):
- citation_recall@1 (primary): fraction of runs where the model cited the correct paragraph id.
- semantic_recall: fuzzy match on the actual answer content (BLEU/ROUGE + instruction-based classifier).
- kv_miss_rate: percent of expected KV keys that were not used in attention above threshold.
- attention_mass_shift: change in attention mass from anchor spans to sink spans (measured via attention weight proxies / integrated gradients if available).
- latency_p50/p95 and decode_tokens_per_sec (to correlate performance SLO degradation with recall loss).
- perplexity_jump_rate: frequency of >X% sudden token-likelihood drops at paragraph boundaries.

Protocol notes / runner commands (quick):
- generation harness: tools/runner/retrieval_stress_runner.py --model {model} --context-size {8k,32k,128k} --profile attention,kvcache --retrieval-pattern {sparse,dense,adversarial} --seed {seed} --out results/rf-001/{model}/{pattern}/{context}/run-{stamp}.json
- shard retrieval on client side for 128k to mimic real RAG; include deliberate interleaving of original prompt and retrieved chunks.

Preliminary anecdotal results (dev cluster runs, 2025-02-20 through 2025-02-28):
- open-model-v2-16k at 32k simulated context (via truncation) predictably loses the anchor after ~+12k tokens of retrieval inserts — citation_recall drops to 30% from baseline 92% at 8k.
- open-model-v2-64k shows graceful degradation in sparse pattern, but in dense-chained pattern citation_recall fell to 45% at 32k and 18% at 128k; attention_mass_shift indicates sink spans captured ~38% of top-100 attention mass in worst-case runs.
- experimental-quant-128k: latency p95 increased x2 for 128k runs but interestingly retained higher semantic_recall than open-model-v2-64k in dense-chained cases (maybe quantized kernels preserve longer-range KV coherency).

Failure-mode sketches (notes to self):
- Truncation vs eviction: observed cases where the model hasn't simply dropped earliest tokens but reallocated attention to recent retrieved duplicates — effectively the old anchor remains in KV physically but receives near-zero attention. Label these as 'soft eviction'.
- Sink amplification: repeating noisy paragraphs with shared tokens (e.g., common stopwords + repeated named entity tokens) cause attention reweighting where a small set of tokens in sink paragraphs attract disproportionate attention across layers.
- Prompt anchoring fragility: when anchor is short (1–2 sentences) and retrieval chain contains paraphrases, the model prefers paraphrased matches over exact anchor unless anchor has explicit id markers. So ID tagging is critical to measure true retrieval fidelity.

Prompt sets (canonical cases - short examples):
- Anchor + single-step Q (control, 8k):
  ANCHOR{id: P0}
  "Dr. Elgin defined wampum as 'X' in paragraph P0."

  PROMPT: "According to paragraph P0, what is wampum defined as? Please cite paragraph id."

- Dense chain (8 -> 32 -> 128 scale):
  Build 40 snippets: each snippet 200–400 tokens, overlap(window) = 30–60% with previous; insert anchor at snippet 5; ask citation Q referencing an attribute only present in snippet 5.

- Adversarial sink insertion: every 5th snippet is a 300-token pseudo-random high-entropy token blob (generated from Markov variants of a legal dump) but with repeated entity tokens like "AcmeCo" inserted 4x to act as attention magnets.

Data collection format: JSONL with fields: run_id, model, pattern, context_size, seed, prompt_id, citation_expected, citation_predicted, semantic_score, latency_ms_p95, attention_mass_top100_sink_pct. (Runner maps to these keys; postprocess notebooks produce summary tables.)

Quick results table snapshot (raw numbers are from early runs on dev-GPU-pool):
- open-model-v2-16k | sparse | 8k -> citation_recall: 0.92 | semantic_recall: 0.95 | p95_latency: 420ms
- open-model-v2-16k | dense  | 32k -> citation_recall: 0.30 | semantic_recall: 0.62 | p95_latency: 610ms
- open-model-v2-64k | dense  | 128k -> citation_recall: 0.18 | semantic_recall: 0.40 | attention_sink_top100: 0.38
- experimental-quant-128k | adversarial | 128k -> citation_recall: 0.42 | semantic_recall: 0.68 | p95_latency: 1.1s

Open questions / next probes (TODOs):
- Add fine-grained layerwise attention logging (need instrumentation changes in runtime; raised PR #812 but still blocked on perf).
- Test with anchor length variations (1s, 3s, 6s) to quantify anchoring sensitivity curve.
- Try explicit non-overlapping ID tokens (UUID-style) vs human-readable ids — does id token entropy help resist paraphrase theft?
- Run longer seeds for parity (N=50 runs per cell) — current N=8–12 noisy.
- Explore cache-aware batching interactions: when we batch heavy 128k requests, do KV shared buffers cause cross-request contamination? (SRE asked to simulate in dedicated env).

Communications / where to look next:
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/srv-runtime/pull/812 (profiling hooks for token attention summary)
- Slack thread: #apl-long-context (see thread dated 2025-02-21 labeled "sink-probe initial" )
- Related issues: JIRA-ENG-APL-2421 (tracking retention-fadecase experiment)

Appendix: raw prompt examples (copy/paste friendly)
- ANCHOR snippet (P0):
  "P0_id:ZQ-127
  Dr. Elgin's taxonomy distinguishes wampum as a ritualized shell bead used as both currency and mnemonic device in treaty-making ceremonies."

- Example retrieval chain generator note (pseudo):
  for i in range(40):
    base = make_paragraph(200, topic=legal_text if i%7==0 else general)
    if i == 5: base = anchor_paragraph
    if i % 5 == 0: base = inject_sink_blob(base)
    output.append( paraphrase(base, overlap_pct=random(30,60)) )

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally terse; aim is to capture early empirical signals and to provide a reproducible recipe for the stress harness. Please comment on: missing metrics, whether the data schema is sufficient for downstream dashboards, and any suggestions for better adversarial sink construction.
- If you want raw run artifacts, look in gs://redwood-dev-evals/rf-001/ (dev-only) or ping me for transfer to long-term bucket.

-- Aisha
